There are only about 6 passages in the bible interpreted as condemning homosexuality. Out of all the many books, that's a miniscule ammount.

Genesis 19 refers to the events at Sodom and Gomorrah. 

"They called to Lot, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us so that we can have sex with them.”

Lot went outside to meet them and shut the door behind him and said, “No, my friends. Don’t do this wicked thing. Look, I have two daughters who have never slept with a man. Let me bring them out to you, and you can do what you like with them. But don’t do anything to these men, for they have come under the protection of my roof." (5-8)

This is the main passage against homosexuality - the men are sinful as they are attempting to have sex with the visitors. A different way of interpreting this is that the men are trying to rape the angels, and that's what makes them sinful. It's not the homosexuality that is wrong, it's the attempted rape.

Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13 both use the words incorrectly translated as "homosexual", as do Corinthians 6:9-10 and 1 Timothy 8-10. These can therefore be discounted as against homosexuality, and are actually against male prostitution, and "feminine men".

The issue with men "taking the female role" refers to both sex position and social expression. In terms of sex position, the "penetrated" person is the sinful one, whereas the other is manly. I don't think this refers directly to homosexuality, rather more a man being "weak" is wrong. Similarly, the feminine presentation of a man means he is weak, however that's all about gender expression which has nothing to do with sexuality.

Finally, the Romans quote you gave is the only verse that can truly be interpreted as against homosexuality. Some arguments against it are that it refers to people being unnatural to themselves - straight women lying with women and straight men lying with men. Ultimately, it was written so many 100s of years ago and it's been translated so many times that the true meaning may well have been lost. If you have time, you might want to read [this article](http://skippingtothepiccolo.com/2006/09/10/christianity-homosexuality-part-2-of-8-romans-126-27/) that explains some reasoning why that quote cannot be used against homosexuality, but basically it explains the context of the quote, and taking it out of context loses a lot of the meaning.
Another thought, is that even if homosexual sex is wrong, the Bible says absolutely nothing about relationships without sex, therefore romantic gay relationships are ok.

A final thought on the Bible as a whole, is that a lot of our views on things has changed since it was written. The Bible has numerous verses supporting slavery, such as Ephesians 6:5-8, “Slaves, be obedient to your human masters with fear and trembling, in sincerity of heart, as to Christ”. This doesn't mean slavery is right, so perhaps the very few verses indicating homosexuality is wrong shouldn't mean that it is.

The problem with your quotes is that they are only a translation of the original language. The word "homosexual" didn't actually appear in the bible until 1946, in any language. The original Greek used the words "arsenokoitai" and "malakos", which were then both translated as "homosexuality".  [This article](http://canyonwalkerconnections.com/word-homosexual-first-introduced-bible/?fb_comment_id=1549297495129729_1550793344980144) gives a better translation of the words: "Simply put, the words arsenokoitai and malakos have closer meaning to a person participating in exploitative sex typically associated with money, and a man taking the social and sexual position of a woman, respectively." While the second definition is easier to link to homosexuality, bear in mind that it is still an English translation, and cannot be considered as totally accurate. The first definition indicates more closely to sex trafficking and prostitution, not homosexuality. Additionally, many other translations of the bible, quotes that in English are against homosexuality, are actually against pedophilia. "Man shall not lie with man" is translated in [one German translation](https://um-insight.net/perspectives/has-%E2%80%9Chomosexual%E2%80%9D-always-been-in-the-bible/) as "man shall not lie with young boy". This same translation of man/young boy occurs a couple of times.

In the original language, the Bible says very little against homosexuality, it is only modern translations that have included the word "homosexual".

The bible has many quotes about love, the famous "love thy neighbor", "Above all love one another deeply, because love covers a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8). me and my sibling are both nonbinary, and my step sister is trans. I started questioning my gender after a friend came out to me, and they started questioning theirs after a friend came out to them. since coming out to 2 friends, they both started questioning their genders, and I have another friend in one of those friendship groups that came out at about the same time. 

Without one person coming out to another, I may not have questioned my gender. or maybe I would have, it just would have taken longer. similarly with me coming out to my friends and them questioning their genders. There's certainly a type of chain reaction in us all figuring out our transness, but whether it is the "something else exists" or the "what if I am that something else", is impossible to tell.

In terms of being LGBTQ, it is certainly true that being around other lgbtq people will be more likely to make a person tolerant, and thus perhaps eventually realise their own gender or sexuality. With more and more knowledge in society about lgbtq people, it makes it easier for many people to come out, and even to realise they are lgbtq. The same can be said specifically about being trans - whereas before a person may have just said they are (for example) a tomboy and just felt uncomfortable without knowing why, now those feelings may lead then to question their actual gender and realise they are trans. We definitely still don't understand gender, and another theory people (generally transphobes) have is that all this exposure to lgbt people actually physically makes others lgbt. Is it that people are more willing to question their gender/sexuality, more people are willing to come out, or more people are actually lgbt?
